extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners interested in the theory and practice of comedy, wit, and literary humour
extracted.subtask_short: theory of the comic in words
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains theoretical criteria for producing and analysing comic effects in situations and in language (wit, parody, pun, transposition, etc.), with examples and methods for turning ideas/phrases into humour. Intended as a guide for analysing or crafting comic writing and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of series
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effect arises when two independent series of events are made to coincide or interfere, producing momentary cross-purposes (e.g., transposing Bonivard and Tartarin into the same situation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build two separate series (contemporary or past vs present) and contrive a partial coincidence; use independent groups thrown into unconnected surroundings; create a smaller comedy within the principal one so one series threatens to upset the other and then is restored. Examples: Labiche’s technique of constructing series separately then making them interfere; mock-heroic transposition from ancient to modern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life / absentmindedness in events
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous in events is 'absentmindedness in things' — life treated as a repeating, reversible mechanism leads to comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain comedy by repeating, inverting, or transferring sets of actions/relations so life 'forgets itself' and appears mechanical. Recognize that this is an artificial exaggeration of a natural rigidity; used especially in light comedy to create a game-like, conventional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: comic expressed vs comic created by language
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate comic that could be translated (comic expressed) from comic that depends on sentence structure/word choices and thus resists translation (comic in words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting/analysing humour, determine whether the effect relies on situational content (translatable) or linguistic structure (syntax, morphology, idiom). The latter requires attention to language-specific forms and often cannot be transferred intact to another language or culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit as the comic in a volatile state / dramatic thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit (esprit) is the comic in a fleeting, volatile form; a 'dramatic' way of thinking that puts ideas on stage, makes them converse like persons, and produces quick comic scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create wit, allow ideas to interact rapidly and economically as if onstage; aim for subtle, delicate, immediate sketches of comic scenes. Understand that wit often reveals the thinker behind the line (less self-forgetfulness than in poetry). Examples: quick repartee, paradoxical twists, miniature 'robber robbed' scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic method for witty remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: To analyse a witty remark: enlarge it into a full scene, determine which category of the comic the scene belongs to, and reduce the witticism to its simplest elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this method both analytically (to explain why a remark is funny) and practically (to expand a one-line witticism into a scene for greater effect). Example: Mme. de Sévigné’s 'Your chest hurts me' enlarged into Molière’s medical scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic via automatism in language / ready-made phrase + absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic meaning is obtained when an absurd idea is fitted into a well-established phrase-form, signalling automatism/utterer’s inelasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit stereotyped phrase-endings or clichéd formulas by inserting an absurdity that makes the automatism obvious (e.g., 'Ce sabre est le plus beau jour de ma vie'). Use dovetailed commonplace phrases to lull attention and then reveal absurdity for comic effect (Labiche examples). This is a major device for comicising a speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalising figurative language (material vs moral meanings)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect arises when an expression used figuratively is intentionally (or pretended to be) taken literally — i.e., attention is fixed on the material side of a metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metaphors where the concrete reading yields an incongruous image (e.g., 'Tous les arts sont frères' -> literalise kinship). Use less-familiar figurative words (e.g., 'cousins' instead of 'brothers') to increase comic tinge. Build rejoinders that force the audience to picture the literal scene (sport metaphors made vividly concrete).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trapping interlocutor by extending their idea (metaphor turned against speaker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit often consists in extending an interlocutor’s idea so they are made to say its contrary or are 'caught' by their own words — typically by exploiting the concrete aspect of a metaphor/comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen for metaphors/comparisons and craft replies that push the literal/concrete implication to the point of absurdity. Example patterns: take a common expression and extend it logically to a ridiculous conclusion, or supply a concrete image that contradicts the speaker’s intended abstract meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words / pun and reciprocal interference in a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy can be produced by allowing two independent meanings to coexist in the same sentence (reciprocal interference); the pun is the least reputable form (homophony), while higher forms use a single sentence expressing genuinely dual meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish levels: puns (sound-based) are crude; play-on-words exploiting polysemy or figurative/literal tension is subtler. Use ambiguity of word-meaning or bracketed independent meanings to create multiplicity of interpretations and thereby humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three fundamental transformations of sentences: repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied to language, comic effects follow three laws: a sentence reversed still makes sense (inversion), a single sentence expresses two independent idea-sets (reciprocal interference), or an expression is transposed into a different key (repetition/transposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating comic sentences, try: (a) inversion (swap grammatical roles to create a new meaning), (b) constructing sentences that genuinely carry two coherent senses, and (c) transposing the natural expression into a different stylistic or social key to make the audience mentally supply the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (subject/object swap) as a comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Inversion consists in reversing parts of a sentence (e.g., subject/object) to yield a comic reinterpretation; it is relatively easy to apply but less profound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inversion for repartee and refutation; test phrases for reversed-meaning possibilities and exploit surface symmetry (e.g., 'What do you mean by emptying your pipe on my terrace?' -> 'What do you mean by putting your terrace under my pipe?'). Best for quick retorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition of natural expression into another key
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect is always obtainable by transposing the natural expression of an idea into another key (e.g., solemn <-> familiar). Transposition is to language what repetition is to comedy in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a target key (solemn, familiar, technical, juvenile, bureaucratic, etc.) and restate an idea in that key when it 'belongs' elsewhere. The audience spontaneously supplies the natural counterpart, producing the comic contrast. This device ranges from buffoonery to lofty irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody (solemn -> familiar transposition / degradation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody results from transposing the solemn into the familiar — making something dignified appear mean or trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use elevated diction for trivial subjects or bring classical/poetic style to modern, vulgar, or mundane topics. Beware: degradation is only one form of transposition; parody is effective when the clash between expected dignity and low subject is clear (e.g., describing dawn 'like a lobster being boiled').

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration / mock-heroic (small -> large transposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating small things as if they were large (or vice versa) — prolonged, systematic exaggeration — creates comic effect; mock-heroic is a recognized form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain exaggeration methodically to create mock-heroic tone; braggadocio often becomes laughable because of its mock-heroic aspect. Use extended hyperbole in style/register to emphasize contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevating the disreputable into respectable language (upward moral transposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing scandalous, low-class, or disgraceful behaviour in 'reputable' or elevated language produces comedy by revealing a moral organisation of immorality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply formal, officious, or bureaucratic diction to corrupt or vulgar acts to expose absurdity (example: 'Your peculations are too extensive for an official of your rank'). Short, well-chosen words can suffice if they suggest an entire system of transposition accepted in certain social circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony vs Humour (real vs ideal transposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony: state what ought to be and pretend you believe it is being done (transposition from ideal to real) — oratorical. Humour: describe what actually is and pretend you believe it ought to be done (transposition from moral to scientific) — scientific, concrete, delights in technical detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce irony, invoke lofty standards and feign their fulfilment; to produce humour, catalogue concrete, detailed facts of the bad/absurd reality with cool, dissector-like detachment. Recognize humour as moral observation disguised as scientific description; irony emphasises the ideal and can become high-pressure eloquence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition/transposition of style as a source of linguistic comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition (in action) corresponds in language to transposition of expression into a different style or 'key' while preserving mutual relations of ideas; the contrast with the natural expression supplies the humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present an idea in an unexpected stylistic register (e.g., legalese, bureaucratese, poetic diction) that contrasts with the idea’s natural expression; let the audience mentally supply the original, enhancing the comic effect. No need to show both forms explicitly — the invented form is often sufficient.
